description_full: The Cheesecake Factory Incorporated operates and licenses restaurants in the United States and Canada. It operates bakeries that produce cheesecakes and other baked products for its restaurants, international licensees, third-party bakery customers, external foodservice operators, retailers, and distributors. The company operates restaurants under the brands comprising The Cheesecake Factory, North Italia, Flower Child, and Fox Restaurant Concepts. The Cheesecake Factory Incorporated was founded in 1972 and is headquartered in Calabasas, California.
ceo_bio: Mr. David M. Overton | Founder, Chairman & CEO | Age 79 | Compensation: $2.5M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 48K people. Revenue per employee of $78K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, with revenue growing 6%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $3K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $567 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 32× revenue per employee (elevated relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: The Cheesecake Factory Incorpor is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $5.4B market cap on $3.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 10% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $155M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.03× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 22× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 7.4% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 65% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 3 other valuation measures)
Very elevated short interest (35.7% of float) — sophisticated money is betting against the business
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $25.5M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 9% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Founder-led — owner alignment that often matters more than any incentive plan
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 148% over the past year excluding the latest month.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $66.07 (margin of safety -65%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 19%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $40.70 to $107 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 25.9 vs 18.8, EV/EBITDA 18.9 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 35.1 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 112% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $106 on average, 3% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 9.6%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.04).

ROE of 34% is amplified by 7.5x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($215.7M of cash against $630.1M of debt), with interest covered 21.6x.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.6% over 3 years, 13.6% over 5 years and 6.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
At current returns, reinvesting 55% of profits supports about 8.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 3.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 8.4% on average.
own: Insiders own 7.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 95%.

It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (2.8% in buybacks and 1.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 11.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 35.7% of the float, 6.4 days to cover.
people: With about 48,000 employees, each generates about $78K of revenue, 0.2x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 5.6% a year across its filed history.

The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
